turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): I've just done his obs. Sats are 96 percent on room air, pulse is 96, resps are 22, and the peak flow went 310, then 330, with a best of 340.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. I'm Dr Shah. So you've been a bit wheezy?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, nah, it's nothing. Just a tickle. I nearly didn't come.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): A tickle. Cough, or more than that?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Bit of a cough, and it whistles when I breathe out. Started after a cold. It's not bad.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did the cold start?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, traffic was shocking getting here, the freeway was just—
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, I'll nick a spacer from the cupboard while you—
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Last Tuesday, I reckon. Sniffles and a sore throat, that's gone now. The whistle has only been a couple of days. Three days, maybe.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Wasn't hot at all.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Coughing anything up?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Nah. Dry. Nothing comes up.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Waking you up at night?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Nah, sleep's fine. I'm not really crook.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short of breath on the stairs, anything like that?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes. Not really.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): I won't put that down as a yes, then. Any chest pain?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Not pain. It's just a bit tight in the chest.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, tight as well. Which puffers are you on?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Blue one and the brown one, and I always muddle them. I've been smashing the brown one because that's the reliever, it opens you—
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): The blue one's the reliever. That's salbutamol. Brown is the preventer.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh, wait, I'm talking rubbish. Blue's the one I've been using all day. I've barely touched the brown one. I get the colours backwards.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many times are you using the blue one, and how many puffs?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Like ten— nah, not ten. Maybe five, six times a day. Two puffs, I think, maybe two.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): The brown one is beclomethasone, two puffs morning and night, every day, even when you're well. Has that been happening?

[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Not really, I forget. My sister lives on biotin gummies for her nails, Dad's got a purple Seretide puffer, and Mum's diabetic so she takes metformin. None of that's mine.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Family's medicines aside, any allergies to any medicines?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Nah. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the asthma, how long?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Since I was a kid. Usually it's nothing, don't know what the fuss is. I don't smoke. Well, a durry at the pub sometimes, not heaps.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Occasional cigarettes, noted. Let me listen to your chest. Deep breaths.
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, go on.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Soft wheeze at both bases. Air entry is decent. No crackles.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Did you catch the cricket last night?
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): The one-dayer? Just the end.
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): That last over was ridiculous. I was yelling at the telly.
[SEG0038] person_1 (NURSE): My brother-in-law was there. Reckons the chip queue was longer than the over.
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): Hot one for it, too. I was stuck on the freeway forty minutes getting here, total car park, just replaying it.
[SEG0040] person_1 (NURSE): Been sticky all week. We still haven't got a proper fan at home.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha. Back to your lungs, though.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check I've got this straight. Cold from last Tuesday, sniffles and sore throat both gone, then about three days of dry cough, wheeze, and some chest tightness.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's it. Hardly worth coming in.

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): No fever, no phlegm, sleeping fine, no chest pain, and you're not actually sure about being short of breath. Blue salbutamol maybe two puffs, five or six times a day, and the brown preventer hardly used. Asthma since you were a kid, and the odd cigarette.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think this is your asthma flaring after the virus, not a pneumonia. A peak flow of 340, plus needing the reliever that often, is enough for me to treat it.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Treat it? I feel a bit silly, it's nothing much.

[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm starting prednisolone, 40 milligrams once a day for five days, by mouth, with food. It's a short steroid course to settle the flare. Keep the blue one, two puffs through a spacer when you're wheezy, and if you need it more than every four hours don't sit on it.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): Five days of that? Seems over the top. Yeah, alright.

[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please actually take the brown one, two puffs morning and night, every day, even when you feel fine. I'll see you back here in three days. If you can't finish a sentence, the reliever isn't helping, or you feel faint, go straight to emergency.

features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
